Salman of Saudi Arabia: Salman is the third-oldest living head of state and the oldest living monarch.
In what year was Barack Obama born?
Barack Obama: Barack Hussein Obama II (born August 4, 1961) is an American politician who served as the 44th president of the United States from 2009 to 2017.

Hirohito: Emperor Shōwa (born Hirohito; 29 April 1901 – 7 January 1989) was Emperor of Japan from 25 December 1926 until his death in 1989.

Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh: Philip was born in Greece into the Greek and Danish royal families.

Miss Universe is an annual international major beauty pageant that is run by the Thailand and Mexican-based Miss Universe Organization.

Who founded Christian Social Union in Bavaria?
Christian Social Union in Bavaria: Karl Scharnagl. The Christian Social Union in Bavaria (German:, CSU) is a Christian democratic and conservative political party in Germany.
Thelema: Aleister Crowley. Thelema is a Western esoteric and occult social and spiritual philosophy, and a new religious movement.
In which country was Ashikaga shogunate?
Ashikaga shogunate: Japan. The Ashikaga clan governed Japan from the Imperial capital of Heian-kyō (Kyoto) as de facto military rulers along with the daimyō lords of the samurai class.
Euromaidan: Ukraine. The scope of the protests widened, with calls for the resignation of Yanukovych and the Azarov government.
In which country is Siege of Sarajevo?
Siege of Sarajevo: Bosnia and Herzegovina. The city was initially besieged by the Yugoslav People's Army, before they were replaced by elements of the newly-formed Army of Republika Srpska.
In which country was Tokugawa shogunate?
Tokugawa shogunate: Japan. The Tokugawa shogunate, also known as the Edo shogunate, was the military government of Japan during the Edo period from 1603 to 1868.
In which country was the Kingdom of Prussia?
Kingdom of Prussia: German Empire. The Kingdom of Prussia (German: Königreich Preußen, pronounced [ˈkøːnɪkʁaɪç ˈpʁɔʏsn̩]) was a German state that existed from 1701 to 1918.
In which country was the Achaemenid Empire?
Achaemenid Empire: Medo-Persia. At peak, its territorial extent was roughly 5.5 million square kilometres (2.1 million square miles), making it the largest empire of its time.

Red Terror: Russian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic. Volodarsky in alleged retaliation for Bolshevik mass repressions, the Red Terror was modeled on the Reign of Terror of the French Revolution, and the Paris Commune.
In which country is Battles of Narvik?
Battles of Narvik: Norway. Narvik provided an ice-free harbour in the North Atlantic for iron ore transported by rail from Kiruna in Sweden.
In which country is Conservative Party based?
Conservative Party (UK): United Kingdom. The Conservative and Unionist Party, commonly the Conservative Party and colloquially the Tories, is a political party in the United Kingdom.

Kingdom of León: Latin. The Kingdom of León was an independent kingdom situated in the northwest region of the Iberian Peninsula.

Sillan. Silla, along with Paekche and Goguryeo, formed the Three Kingdoms of Korea.

This countercultural activist helped found the Youth International Party and stood trial as one of the Chicago Seven, though his conviction was later thrown out on appeal — who is he?
Abbie Hoffman (November 30, 1936 - April 12, 1989) was an American political and social activist who co-founded the Youth International Party ("Yippies") and was a member of the Chicago Seven.

Andrei Troshev (born April 5, 1962), nicknamed Sedoi (lit. 'the Grey-Haired'), is a Russian retired colonel and veteran of the Soviet-Afghan War, the Second Chechen War, and the Russian military intervention in the Syrian civil war.
This Indian politician served three non-consecutive terms as Chief Minister of Rajasthan — starting in 1998, 2008, and 2018 — after earlier representing Jodhpur in the national parliament. Who is he?

Ashok Gehlot (born 3 May 1951) is an Indian politician who served as the Chief Minister of Rajasthan from 1998 to December 2003, then again from 2008 to December 2013, and later from 2018 to December 2023.

Sparked by riots in Brussels after a nationalist opera performance in August 1830, this uprising split the mostly Catholic southern provinces from the Dutch-led union to form a new kingdom — which event?

Belgian Revolution was a conflict which led to the secession of the southern provinces (mainly the former Southern Netherlands) from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands and the establishment of an independent Kingdom of Belgium.
Installed as high priest by the Roman procurator Valerius Gratus, this New Testament figure is described as the organizer behind Jesus's trial before the Sanhedrin — who was he?
Caiaphas was a High Priest of Israel during the first century.

This monarch's court physician, Johann Friedrich Struensee, effectively ran Denmark and Norway for two years before being overthrown in an 1772 coup, after which the ruler's own son eventually acted as unofficial regent — who was he?
Christian VII (29 January 1749 - 13 March 1808) was King of Denmark and Norway and Duke of Schleswig and Holstein from 1766 until his death in 1808.
After 37 years in the U.S. Army commanding forces in Iraq and Afghanistan, this four-star general traded the uniform for the spy chief's chair before resigning in 2012 — who is he?

David Petraeus (born 7 November 1952) is a retired United States Army general who served as the fourth director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) from September 2011 until his resignation in November 2012.
Son of a chambermaid and a carpenter, this British politician led the Conservatives, served as PM from 1970 to 1974, and was also a keen yachtsman and musician — who is he?
Edward Heath (9 July 1916 - 17 July 2005) was a British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1970 to 1974 and Leader of the Conservative Party from 1965 to 1975.
On 30 April 1975, North Vietnamese forces under General Van Tien Dung captured South Vietnam's capital, triggering a frantic evacuation and ending the Vietnam War — what is this event called?

Fall of Saigon was captured by North Vietnam on 30 April 1975. The aftermath ushered in a transition period under the Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam until the formal reunification in 1976.
Described by Homer as the most handsome of mortals, this Trojan youth was abducted by the gods to become Zeus's cup-bearer on Olympus — who is he?
Ganymede (mythology) (Ancient) is a divine hero whose homeland was Troy.

The first Democrat elected president after the Civil War, this former Buffalo mayor and New York governor holds a unique distinction: he's the only president to serve two nonconsecutive terms. Who was he?
Grover Cleveland (March 18, 1837 - June 24, 1908) was the 22nd and 24th president of the United States, serving from 1885 to 1889 and from 1893 to 1897.
A Jewish refugee who fled Nazi Germany in 1938, which Harvard-trained diplomat later served as national security advisor and secretary of state under Nixon and Ford?
Henry Kissinger (May 27, 1923 - November 29, 2023) was an American diplomat, political scientist, and politician.

This nomadic people swept out of Central Asia into Eastern Europe between the 4th and 6th centuries CE, pushing Goths and Alans westward and building a vast but short-lived empire on Rome's Danube frontier — who were they?

Huns were a nomadic people who lived in Central Asia, the Caucasus, and Eastern Europe between the 4th and 6th centuries CE. By 370 CE, the Huns had arrived on the Volga, causing the westwards movement of Goths and Alans.
Sailing from Brittany, this explorer charted the Saint Lawrence River and gave a nation its name using the Iroquoian term for the villages at Stadacona and Hochelaga — who is he?
Jacques Cartier (31 December 1491 - 1 September 1557) was a French maritime explorer from Brittany.
Appointed by George W. Bush as ambassador to the United Nations, this attorney and diplomat later returned to government as a national security advisor in 2018 — who is he?
John Bolton (born November 20, 1948) is an American attorney, diplomat, Republican consultant, and political commentator.
This Polish statesman became the country's first Marshal and is regarded as the father of a republic re-established in 1918, 123 years after Poland had last been partitioned — who is he?
Józef Piłsudski (5 December 1867 - 12 May 1935) was a Polish statesman who served as the Chief of State (1918-1922) and first Marshal of Poland (from 1920).
This Soviet politician led the USSR for just over a year, from February 1984 until his death in March 1985, capping a career that began in Komsomol propaganda work. Who is he?
Konstantin Chernenko was Leader of the Soviet Union from 1984 to 1985.

This 16th-century struggle for a Baltic territory saw Russia's early gains at Narva and Dorpat eventually checked by an alliance of Sweden, Denmark-Norway, and Poland-Lithuania — what's this conflict known as?
Livonian War (1558-1583) concerned the control of Old Livonia (in the territory of present-day Estonia and Latvia).
Working as a nurse in New York's slums, this campaigner for legal contraception helped develop the first birth control pill and founded a major reproductive-health organization — who is she?
Margaret Sanger (ne Higgins; September 14, 1879 - September 6, 1966) was an American birth control activist, sex educator, writer, and nurse.
Called 'the defining event of modern' this country's history, it raged from 1910 to 1920 and put revolutionary generals in power for the next two decades — what was it?
Mexican Revolution was an extended sequence of armed regional conflicts in Mexico from 20 November 1910 to 1 December 1920.
This Hebrew prophet led his enslaved people out of Egypt and, according to scripture, received a divine law that became part of the Torah — who is he?
Moses was the Hebrew prophet who led the Israelites out of slavery in the Exodus from Egypt.
This Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin appears only in the Gospel of John, where he's drawn to Jesus's teachings and, some traditions hold, becomes a secret disciple — who is he?
Nicodemus is a New Testament figure venerated as a saint in a number of Christian traditions.

A Waffen-SS commando who helped rescue Benito Mussolini in the daring Gran Sasso raid, this operative later led Operation Greif, infiltrating German soldiers behind Allied lines in enemy uniforms, and was acquitted at a 1947 war-crimes tribunal — who is he?
Otto Skorzeny (12 June 1908 - 5 July 1975) was an Austrian-born German in the Waffen-SS during World War II.
Elevated to Cabinet Minister in 2017 and later India's longest-serving Commerce and Industry chief, which politician once led the Rajya Sabha as Leader of the House?
Piyush Goyal (born 13 June 1964) is an Indian politician who is serving as the 13th Minister of Commerce and Industry since 2019, also being the longest serving minister for the same.

This American politician made history as the first Palestinian American woman elected to Congress, and was one of the first two Muslim women ever elected to the body, alongside Ilhan Omar — who is she?

This Shia cleric led a 1979 revolution that overthrew Mohammad Reza Pahlavi and transformed a country into an Islamic republic. Who was he?
Ruhollah Khomeini (17 May 1900 - 3 June 1989) was an Iranian politician and Shia cleric who served as the first supreme leader of Iran from 1979 until his death in 1989.
Fluent in Sinhala and Dhivehi from his early diplomatic postings in Sri Lanka, this Russian official has served as foreign minister since 2004, longer than anyone since the Soviet era — who is he?
Sergey Lavrov (born 21 March 1950) is a Russian diplomat who has served as Minister of Foreign Affairs since 2004.
After unexpectedly beating Effie Achtsioglou for the leadership of Greece's Syriza party in 2023, which politician later founded Democrats - Progressive Center?
Stefanos Kasselakis (born 29 March 1988) is a Greek businessman, entrepreneur and politician who previously served as the leader of Syriza.

This de facto independent East Asian state emerged after the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912, drew rival British and Russian interest, and lost its independence to the People's Republic of China in 1951 — which state?
Tibet (1912–1951) was a de facto independent state in East Asia that lasted from the collapse of the Qing dynasty in 1912 until its annexation by the People's Republic of China in 1951.
This Indian Army captain was posthumously awarded the Param Vir Chakra, India's highest military honor, after being killed fighting at Point 4875 during the 1999 Kargil War — who is he?
Vikram Batra (9 September 1974 - 7 July 1999) was an Indian Army officer.

He was the last U.S. president to have fought in the Civil War — the only one who started as an enlisted man and finished a brevet major — before leading the nation into the Spanish-American War and an assassin's bullet in 1901. Which president?
William McKinley (January 29, 1843 - September 14, 1901) was the 25th president of the United States, serving from 1897 until his assassination in 1901.
As Guatemala's president from 1996 to 2000, this leader signed the peace accord that ended a 36-year civil war — and was elected mayor of the capital on six separate occasions; who is he?

Álvaro Arzú (14 March 1946 - 27 April 2018) was a Guatemalan politician and businessman who served as the 44th president of Guatemala from 1996 to 2000, as well as several terms as Mayor of Guatemala City.

Alboin: King of the Lombards from c. 560 to 572.

The seventh pharaoh of Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty inherited a vast kingdom from his father Thutmose III but fought far less, his reign seeing hostilities with Mitanni effectively cease — which ruler was he?
Amenhotep II: Seventh Pharaoh of the Eighteenth dynasty of Egypt. Amenhotep II (lit. '"Amun is Satisfied"'), also called Amenophis II, was the seventh pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt.

An international decentralized activist collective born on 4chan in 2003, operating as a 'global brain' or 'hivemind'—they've targeted everyone from governments to the Church of Scientology. What is this loose-knit group called?
Anonymous (hacker group): Decentralized hacktivist collective. Evaluations of the group's actions and effectiveness vary widely.
Founded around the city of Assur circa 2600 BC, this Mesopotamian power grew from city-state to empire and is divided by historians into Old, Middle and Neo- periods — which civilization is it?
Assyria: Major Mesopotamian civilization. The remaining Assyrian people, who have survived in northern Mesopotamia to modern times, were gradually Christianized from the 1st century AD onward.
In 53 BC, seven Roman legions under Crassus were lured into the desert and crushed by Parthian cataphracts and horse archers near a town in modern-day Turkey — what was this military clash called?
Battle of Carrhae: Part of the Roman–Parthian Wars.
This physical theory explains the cosmic microwave background and the abundance of light elements, placing the universe's initial singularity around 13.787 billion years ago. What is it?
Big Bang: Physical theory of the cosmos. The Big Bang is a physical theory that describes how the universe expanded from an initial state of high density and temperature.

Founded in 1978 by Jacques Saadé and headquartered in a namesake tower in Marseille, this French firm is the world's third-largest container shipping company, running nearly 600 vessels — which company?
CMA CGM: French shipping company. CMA CGM operations include shipping, port operation, supply chain management, and warehousing.

Champaran Satyagraha: First civil resistance movement led by Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi in India in 1917.

Cyril Ramaphosa: President of South Africa since 2018. A former anti-apartheid activist and trade union leader, Ramaphosa is also the president of the African National Congress (ANC).

This ancient Athenian orator first took the stand at age 20 to win back his inheritance from his own guardians, before becoming a professional speechwriter and, by 354 BC, a political voice — who is he?
Demosthenes: Classical Athenian statesman and orator (384–322 BC)
This historical era of a major world religion ran from its origins in the Levant among Jewish and Phoenician converts up to the First Council of Nicaea in 325 AD — which era?

Early Christianity: Historical era of the Christian religion. Early Christianity, otherwise called the Early Church, describes the historical era of the Christian religion up to the First Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.
Venerated as a prophet in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, this Hebrew Bible wonder-worker advised the kings of Judah and was hailed as 'the chariots of Israel and its horsemen' — who is he?
Elisha: Prophet and wonder-worker in the Hebrew Bible. Before he settled in Samaria, Elisha passed some time on Mount Carmel.
Her name means 'living one' or 'source of life,' and some scholars link it to an Aramaic word for snake — who was the first woman in the Book of Genesis?
Eve: First woman according to the Abrahamic creation myth.
Owned by the government of the United Arab Emirates, this budget carrier flies to 131 destinations across the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and Europe and its slogan is 'Get Going' — which airline?
Flydubai: Airline of the United Arab Emirates. The airline mainly operates out of Terminal 2 at Dubai International Airport, though some flights fly out from Terminal 3.
The fifth president of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, this leader succeeded his late father as head of the country's oldest political party before winning a disputed 2018 election — who is he?
Félix Tshisekedi: President of the Democratic Republic of the Congo since 2019.
A French knight who fought alongside Joan of Arc in 1429, this nobleman is chiefly remembered for his later conviction for the rape and murder of numerous children — who was he?
Gilles de Rais: Medieval French nobleman and convicted serial killer.

After a failed plot to kidnap Eleanor of Aquitaine got him banished from Poitou, this Frankish knight became king of Jerusalem through marriage to Queen Sibylla, only to lose the kingdom to Saladin — who was he?
Guy of Lusignan: King of Jerusalem from 1186 to 1192.
Formed in 2017 from a merger of Islamist factions, this group led the offensive that toppled the Syrian government in December 2024 — which organization?
Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham: Sunni Islamist and Jihadist military and political organisation.
On a May evening in 1937, a hydrogen-filled German airship burst into flames while docking in New Jersey, killing 35 of the 97 aboard — by what name is this catastrophe known?
Hindenburg disaster: 1937 airship fire in the US.
In existence from 1949 to 1989 and bordering Romania, Czechoslovakia, and Yugoslavia, this Soviet-aligned state saw a major uprising in 1956 — what was this Cold War government called?
Hungarian People's Republic: Country in Central Europe (1949–1989)
Rising from vice president to head of state after her husband's death in 1974, this Argentine leader became the first woman ever to serve as a country's president — who was she?
Isabel Perón: President of Argentina from 1974 to 1976.
Crowned as a child after his father died at the siege of Roxburgh Castle, this unpopular King of Scots faced two major rebellions and died at the Battle of Sauchieburn in 1488 — who was he?
James III of Scotland: King of Scots from 1460 to 1488.
A two-time NCAA wrestling champion before entering politics, this Ohio congressman helped found the House Freedom Caucus and now chairs the House Judiciary Committee — who is he?
A philologist with a Heidelberg doctorate, he became the Gauleiter of Berlin and the Nazi Party's chief propagandist before his 1945 suicide. Who is he?
Joseph Goebbels: German Nazi propaganda minister (1897–1945)
Known as the "Merrie Monarch" for his singing and ukulele playing, this last king of Hawaiʻi lifted the public ban on hula — who was he?
Kalākaua: King of Hawaii from 1874 to 1891.
Schooled at an international academy in Switzerland before inheriting power in 2011, which dictator became the third of his family to rule North Korea?
Kim Jong Un: Leader of North Korea since 2011.
French for 'let do,' this economic philosophy holds that markets self-regulate best when free from subsidies and government regulation — what's it called?
Laissez-faire: Economic system free from interventionism.
The only queen regnant and last sovereign of the Hawaiian Kingdom, deposed in an 1893 coup, she composed 'Aloha ʻOe' and wrote her autobiography during her imprisonment — who was she?
Liliʻuokalani: Queen of Hawaii from 1891 to 1893.

This Mexican politician served as mayor of Mexico City from 2006 to 2012, where he launched the Ecobici bike-share system, before later becoming the country's secretary of foreign affairs — who is he?
Countess in her own right and queen consort to King Stephen, her courage and determination are credited by historians with keeping him on the English throne through the Anarchy. Who was she?
Matilda of Boulogne: Queen of England from 1135 to 1152.
Spanning roughly the 5th to late 15th centuries, this era began with the fall of the Western Roman Empire and gave way to the Renaissance. Which historical period is this?
Middle Ages: European history from the 5th to 15th centuries.
This BJP politician has served as Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh while representing the Ujjain South constituency since 2013 — who is he?
Mohan Yadav: Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh (born 1965)

Crowned King of Rome at birth and later nicknamed 'the Eaglet,' he was the disputed Emperor of the French for all of two weeks in 1815 before living out his days in Vienna — which son of a famous conqueror?
Napoleon II: Disputed Emperor of the French in 1815 (1811–1832)
Nicknamed the 'Expressway Man of India' for spearheading projects like the Mumbai-Pune Expressway, this politician has served as Minister of Road Transport since 2014 — who is he?
Ruling Sweden and Norway from 1872, this monarch saw his joint crown split apart in 1905 when Norway's throne passed to a Danish prince — who was he?
Oscar II: King of Sweden (1872–1907) and Norway (1872–1905)
Fought from 431 to 404 BC, this clash between Athens's Delian League and Sparta's league turned only when Persia backed the Spartans — what conflict is it?
Peloponnesian War: War between Athens and Sparta (431–404 BC). The war consists of four related conflicts which have traditionally been combined into one.

Ruling Mexico for more than three decades until his 1911 overthrow, this general-turned-dictator once studied for the priesthood before switching to law under the mentorship of future president Benito Juárez. Who is he?
Porfirio Díaz: President and Dictator of Mexico from 1876 to 1911.
A chartered accountant turned politician, this Rajya Sabha member spent years as an outspoken Aam Aadmi Party figure before defecting to the BJP in April 2026 — who is he?
Born in 1994, this German politician led the Green Youth, then served as her party's women's-policy spokeswoman before becoming co-leader of the Greens in 2022 — who is she?
Ricarda Lang: German politician (born 1994). Ricarda Lang (born 17 January 1994) is a German politician of the Alliance 90/The Greens who has been serving as a member of the Bundestag since 2021.
This August 1992 siege in Boundary County, Idaho began when U.S. Marshals came to arrest Randy Weaver — over a sawed-off shotgun sale — after he was given the wrong court date. What event was it?
Ruby Ridge standoff: 1992 siege and shootout in Idaho, US.
A former partisan and socialist politician, this journalist-turned-statesman served as president of Italy from 1978 to 1985 — who is he?
Sandro Pertini: President of Italy from 1978 to 1985.
Serving as his country's foreign minister since 2004 — longer than anyone since the Soviet era — this diplomat also speaks fluent Sinhala and Dhivehi from his early postings — who is he?
This legendary Germanic hero slew the dragon Fafnir and was later murdered after a quarrel involving his wife and another woman he had unknowingly helped deceive — who is he?
Writing under the pseudonym 'Frank Talk,' this South African activist led the grassroots Black Consciousness Movement against apartheid in the late 1960s and 1970s — who is he?
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley
Steve Biko: South African anti-apartheid activist (1946–1977)
Described in its founding text as formless, eternal, and the 'Mother of the universe,' this East Asian philosophical concept's Chinese character means 'the way' or 'path' — what is it?
Tao: Philosophical concept native to China.
Cao Wei, Shu Han and Eastern Wu carved up China between 220 and 280 AD after the collapse of the Han dynasty — what is this era called?
Three Kingdoms: Period of Chinese history from 220 to 280 CE.

Born in Ohio and originally named Hiram, this West Point graduate led the Vicksburg campaign that seized control of the Mississippi River before becoming the Union's top general and eventually the 18th U.S. president — who is he?
Ulysses S. Grant: Civil War general, U.S. president from 1869 to 1877.
While imprisoned at Ratnagiri in 1923, this Indian politician coined the Hindu-nationalist ideology of Hindutva and had earlier co-founded a secret society called Abhinav Bharat — who was he?
Vinayak Damodar Savarkar: Indian politician and ideologue (1883–1966)
This Luftwaffe ace was the first pilot in history to down 100 enemy aircraft and devised the famous finger-four formation — yet he died as a passenger in a plane crash. Who was he?
Werner Mölders: German World War II flying ace.
Son of Darius the Great and a grandson of Cyrus the Great, this Achaemenid King of Kings is best remembered for his doomed 480 BC invasion of Greece — who?
Xerxes I: King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire from 486 to 465 BC.
As the first Premier of the People's Republic of China, he helped orchestrate Richard Nixon's landmark 1972 visit while also serving as foreign minister during the 1950s — who is he?
Zhou Enlai: Premier of China from 1949 to 1976.

Marie Curie is a physicist. Curie was born in Warsaw, Russian Empire, where she studied at the clandestine Flying University and began her practical scientific training.
Which of these is a chemist?
Alfred Nobel is a chemist. Alfred Bernhard Nobel ( noh-BEL; Swedish: [ˈǎlːfrɛd nʊˈbɛlː]; 21 October 1833 – 10 December 1896) was a Swedish chemist, inventor, engineer, and businessman.
What is the atomic number of Fermium?
Fermium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fm and atomic number 100.
In what year was Neil Armstrong born?
Neil Armstrong: Armstrong was born and raised near Wapakoneta, Ohio.
In what year did Karl Marx die?
Karl Marx: Born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia, Marx earned a doctoral degree in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841.
In what year was Argon discovered?
Argon is a chemical element; it has symbol Ar and atomic number 18.
Which company manufactures Consolidated B-24 Liberator?
Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control
Consolidated B-24 Liberator: North American Aviation. The Consolidated B-24 Liberator is an American heavy bomber, designed by Consolidated Aircraft of San Diego, California.
In which country is Virgo interferometer?
Virgo interferometer: Italy. The Virgo interferometer is a large-scale scientific instrument near Pisa, Italy, for detecting gravitational waves.
Who is credited with discovering Archaea?
Archaea: Carl Woese. Archaea (ar-KEE-ə) is a domain of organisms.
Who is credited with discovering Synapse?
Synapse: Charles Scott Sherrington. In the nervous system, a synapse is a structure that allows a neuron to exchange (receive or send) signals with another cell in its immediate vicinity.
Who is credited with discovering Nitrogen?
Nitrogen: Daniel Rutherford. Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
Known by the abbreviation NAC, this mucolytic drug treats acetaminophen overdose and also loosens thick mucus in people with chronic lung conditions like pneumonia and bronchitis — which drug?

Acetylcysteine (NAC) is a mucolytic that is used to treat paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and to loosen thick mucus in individuals with chronic bronchopulmonary disorders, such as pneumonia and bronchitis.
This amphoteric compound forms a gelatinous precipitate in water and occurs naturally as the mineral gibbsite, one of bauxite's key components — what is it?
Aluminium hydroxide is a white chemical compound that is found as the mineral gibbsite (also known as hydrargillite) and its three much rarer polymorphs: bayerite, doyleite, and nordstrandite.
This lustrous grey metalloid, found mainly in the mineral stibnite, was historically powdered for use as a cosmetic known by its Arabic name, kohl. What element is it?
Antimony is a chemical element with the symbol Sb (from Latin stibium) and atomic number 51.

The third-largest member of its family behind the Siberian taimen and Pacific Chinook, this anadromous fish hatches in rivers, matures at sea, and changes color and appearance when it returns upstream to spawn — name this fish?
Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) is a species of ray-finned fish in the family Salmonidae.
Coined in 1814 by chemist William Hyde Wollaston, this polyatomic anion forms as carbonic acid loses a proton, and plays a crucial role buffering the body's pH — what's the ion?
Bicarbonate (American; nomenclature: hydrogencarbonate) is an intermediate form in the deprotonation of carbonic acid.

Making up only about 2.6 percent of the brain's total weight, this stalk-like structure connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and regulates critical functions like heart rate and breathing. What is it called?
Brainstem (or brain stem) is the posterior stalk-like part of the brain that connects the cerebrum with the spinal cord.

Standing in contrast to the 'cat-like' carnivorans that diversified across Africa and southern Asia, this suborder unites dogs, bears, raccoons, and pinnipeds under one 'dog-like' umbrella — what's it called?
Caniformia is a suborder within the order Carnivora consisting of "dog-like" carnivorans.
First cultivated in Mesoamerica and later spread worldwide during the Columbian Exchange, this edible gourd-family plant is also known as christophine, mirliton, or choko — what is it?

Chayote (previously placed in the obsolete genus Sechium, now in the genus Sicyos, as Sicyos edulis), also known as christophine, mirliton, gisquil, and choko, is an edible plant belonging to the gourd family, Cucurbitaceae.
Mostly belonging to the genus Naja, these venomous snakes are known for rearing upward and flaring a distinctive hood when threatened — name this common snake type?
Cobra is the common name of various venomous snakes, most of which belong to the genus Naja.
Belonging to the same genus as poliovirus and echovirus, these enteroviruses enter cells with help from a shared receptor and commonly cause aseptic meningitis — which pathogens?

Coxsackievirus are a few related enteroviruses that belong to the Picornaviridae family of nonenveloped, linear, positive-sense, single-stranded, RNA viruses, as well as its genus Enterovirus, which also includes poliovirus and echovirus.
This genus of roughly 340 species includes the carnation and the sweet william, and is nicknamed 'pink' — which genus?

Dianthus (dy-) is a genus of about 340 species of flowering plants in the family Caryophyllaceae, native mainly to Europe and Asia, with a few species in northern and southern Africa, and one species (D. repens) in arctic North America.

Dubbed 'the father of public relations' in his obituary, this Austrian-American pioneer orchestrated a famous 1929 campaign branding cigarettes as feminist 'Torches of Freedom' to encourage women to smoke — who was he?

Edward Bernays (bur-NAYZ; Austrian; November 22, 1891 March 9, 1995) was an Austrian-American pioneer in the field of public relations and propaganda, referred to in his obituary as "the father of public relations".
Co-founder of MIT's J-PAL poverty lab, she shared a 2019 Nobel with her husband and Michael Kremer for using randomized trials against global poverty — who is it?

Esther Duflo (born 25 October 1972) is a French-American economist currently serving as the Abdul Latif Jameel Professor of Poverty Alleviation and Development Economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

In English its plural is the same word for many individuals but changes form when you mean many species — a quirk of this gill-bearing, cold-blooded vertebrate that lacks limbs with digits. What is it?
Fish is an aquatic, anamniotic, gill-bearing vertebrate animal with a tough cranium to protect the brain, but lacking limbs with digits.
This field of study examines how a country's physical geography shapes its politics and its relations with other nations — what field is it?
Geopolitics (from Ancient Greek g 'earth, land' and politik 'politics') is the study of the effects of Earth's geography on politics and international relations.
A French polymath dabbling in anthropology, medicine and physics, he's best remembered for an 1895 book that became a seminal work of crowd psychology — who was he?
Gustave Le Bon (7 May 1841 - 13 December 1931) was a leading French polymath whose areas of interest included anthropology, psychology, sociology, medicine, invention, and physics.
Serving as both Reichsbank president and Minister of Economics under Hitler, this economist was credited with Germany's 1930s 'economic miracle' even as he opposed aspects of rearmament — who is he?
Hjalmar Schacht (22 January 1877 - 3 June 1970) was a German economist, banker, politician, and co-founder of the German Democratic Party.

This nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug treats pain, fever, and inflammation — from migraines to arthritis — and typically starts working within an hour, whether taken orally or intravenously. What drug?
Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is used to relieve pain, fever, and inflammation.
With brownish-grey fur and a pinkish-red face, this cold-hardy primate is known colloquially by a wintry nickname referencing the snow in its habitat — which species?
Japanese macaque (Macaca fuscata), also known as the snow monkey, is a terrestrial Old World monkey species that is native to Japan.
Brewed from the root of a Pacific pepper plant and sipped from a communal bowl in island ceremonies, this psychoactive drink takes its bitter-tasting name from Tongan and Marquesan — what is it?
Kava (Piper methysticum: Latin 'pepper' and Latinized Greek 'intoxicating') is a plant in the pepper family, native to the Pacific Islands.
Its pale golden coat is patterned not with simple dots but with dark spots clustered into rings called rosettes, and it has prowled Africa and Asia since the Early Pleistocene — which big cat is it?
Leopard (Panthera pardus) is one of the five extant cat species in the genus Panthera.
This programming language, whose bytecode interpreter is written in ANSI C, was created in 1993 mainly to let developers extend and customize software — which language?
Lua is a lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm programming language designed mainly for embedded use in applications.
Known by a nickname, this Swedish programmer created Minecraft, the best-selling video game in history, and founded the studio Mojang in 2009 — who is he?
Markus Persson (born 1 June 1979), known by the pseudonym Notch, is a Swedish video game programmer and designer.

Credited with discovering both the atmosphere of Venus and the law of conservation of mass in chemical reactions, this Russian polymath was also a poet who helped shape the modern Russian literary language and is considered a founder of modern geology — who is he?
This genus of bacteria lacks a cell wall entirely, making it naturally immune to antibiotics like penicillin that target cell-wall synthesis — name this genus?
Mycoplasma is a genus of bacteria that, like the other members of the class Mollicutes, lack a cell wall (peptidoglycan) around their cell membrane.
Doubling as a hormone, neurotransmitter, and neuromodulator, this catecholamine's very name nods to the kidney — and goes by 'noradrenaline' nearly everywhere outside the United States. What is it?

Norepinephrine (NE), also called noradrenaline (NA) or noradrenalin, is an organic chemical in the catecholamine family that functions in the brain and body as a hormone, neurotransmitter and neuromodulator.

This female reproductive gland produces eggs that travel through the oviduct to the uterus, while also functioning as an endocrine organ that secretes hormones governing the menstrual cycle — what organ is it?
Ovary (from Latin vrium 'egg') is a gonad in the female reproductive system that produces ova; when released, an ovum travels through the oviduct into the uterus.

Classically, one form of this condition wakes you at night with upper abdominal pain that eases when you eat, while another flares up after meals — and a third of older sufferers feel nothing at all. What is it?
Peptic ulcer disease refers to damage of the inner part of the stomach's gastric mucosa (lining of the stomach), the first part of the small intestine, or sometimes the lower esophagus.

Despite its fearsome reputation as a ferocious predator, this South American freshwater fish actually eats a varied diet that includes plant material, making it more omnivore than monster — what fish is it?
Piranha (or) is any of a number of freshwater fish species in the subfamily Serrasalminae, of the family Serrasalmidae, in the order Characiformes.
Including raccoons, coatis, kinkajous, and ringtails, this New World mammal family within the order Carnivora is made up mostly of omnivores — what family is it?
Procyonidae is a New World family of the order Carnivora. Procyonidae ( PROH-see-ON-i-dee) is a New World family of the order Carnivora.

This genus of roughly 1,750 flowering plant species, found worldwide mostly in temperate and mountainous regions, includes a tenacious creeping species common in European gardens as well as bulbous and meadow-dwelling relatives. What are these plants commonly called?
Ranunculus is a large genus of about 1750 species of flowering plants in the family Ranunculaceae.
Caused by two strains of human herpesvirus and nicknamed 'sixth disease,' this common childhood illness brings a rapid fever that gives way to a pink rash within days — what's it called?
Roseola is an infectious disease caused by certain types of human herpes viruses.
Central nervous system depressants in this drug class are often grouped with hypnotics, though technically they're meant to calm rather than induce sleep — what class of drug is this?
Sedative is a substance that induces sedation by reducing irritability or excitement.
With the formula CH3COONa, this colorless, moisture-absorbing salt of acetic acid is deliquescent, meaning it can even dissolve in the water it pulls from the air — which compound?
Sodium acetate is a chemical compound with formula CH3COONa, also abbreviated NaOAc.

This alkaline earth metal, symbol Sr and atomic number 38, shares chemical properties with its periodic-table neighbors calcium and barium, and is mostly mined from the minerals celestine and strontianite — what element is it?
Strontium is a chemical element; it has symbol Sr and atomic number 38. The metal forms a dark oxide layer when it is exposed to air.
Known pharmaceutically as dronabinol, this is the principal psychoactive compound found in cannabis, used medically to relieve chemotherapy-induced nausea. What compound is it?
Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is a cannabinoid found in cannabis.

Stretching from the base of the skull down to the lower back and out to each shoulder blade, this large paired muscle supports the arm and moves the scapula in three distinct ways — what's the muscle?
Trapezius is a large paired trapezoid-shaped surface muscle that extends longitudinally from the occipital bone to the lower thoracic vertebrae of the spine and laterally to the spine of the scapula.
Mammals, birds, amphibians, fish, and reptiles all belong to this subphylum of animals, united by a backbone and a braincase — what is it?
Vertebrate are animals with a vertebral column and a cranium.
Passed only from fathers to sons, this genetic structure carries the SRY gene that typically triggers development of male gonads in mammals — what is it?
Y chromosome is one of two sex chromosomes in therian mammals and other organisms.

Nicknamed wolfsbane, monkshood, and devil's helmet, this highly toxic genus of over 250 mountain-dwelling flowering plants thrives in moist, well-draining soils across the Northern Hemisphere — what is it?
Aconitum: Genus of flowering plants in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae.
Which Swiss chemist was the first person to synthesize and personally experience the effects of LSD, later isolating the active compounds in magic mushrooms?
Native to North America but now invasive across Europe after being introduced, this semiaquatic mustelid preys on rodents, fish, and frogs — which animal?
American mink: Semiaquatic species of mustelid. Because of range expansion, the American mink is classed as a least-concern species by the IUCN.
Native to Africa, India, the Middle East and Central Asia, these fleet-footed members of the family Bovidae aren't actually one single evolutionary group — what are they?
Ranging from a racing tachycardia to a sluggish bradycardia, this catch-all term covers any heartbeat that strays from normal sinus rhythm — what is it called?
Arrhythmia: Group of medical conditions characterized by irregular heartbeat.
This slender projection of a nerve cell typically carries electrical impulses away from the cell body toward other neurons, muscles, or glands — what is it called?
Axon: Long projection on a neuron that conducts signals to other neurons.
Sold under the brand name Tessalon, this cough-relief medication works within about 20 minutes by acting as a local anesthetic that blocks stretch receptors in the lungs — what is this drug called?
Benzonatate: Oral cough medication. Benzonatate, sold under the brand name Tessalon among others, is a medication that is used for the symptomatic relief of cough.
Native to tropical South America, this large non-venomous member of family Boidae is a fixture of private collections thanks to its wildly variable color patterns — what species is it?

After resigning from Evergreen State College following 2017 protests over campus racial equity, this podcaster and former evolutionary biology professor was named part of the 'intellectual dark web' — who is he?
Bret Weinstein: American podcaster and author (born 1969)
Formed when quicklime reacts with water, this compound goes by names like slaked lime and builders' lime, and is used in food prep under the additive code E526 — what is it?
Calcium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Ca(OH)2.

This American Nobel laureate coined the term 'bioorthogonal chemistry' for reactions that work inside living systems, building chemical tools to study the cell-surface sugars called glycans. Who is she?
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like herb is brewed into calming teas and can trigger uterine contractions in its Roman variety — what is it?
Chamomile: Common name for several daisy-like plants.
In this chronic liver condition, healthy tissue is replaced by scar tissue and regenerative nodules, choking blood flow and causing portal hypertension — what is it called?
Cirrhosis: Chronic disease of the liver, characterized by fibrosis.
In mathematics, this is a selection of items from a set where the order of choosing them does not matter, unlike a permutation — what is it called?

Combination: Selection of items from a set. In mathematics, a combination is a selection of items from a set that has distinct members, such that the order of selection does not matter (unlike permutations).
Domesticated in Africa and thriving in sandy, low-rainfall soil, this ancient legume is now grown mostly in Nigeria and Niger, which together supply two-thirds of the world's crop — which plant?
Cowpea: Species of plant. The cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is an annual herbaceous legume from the genus Vigna.
Son of a bass-baritone and born into a family of engineers, this American built his first car at 19, won four F1 Grands Prix, and took Le Mans in 1967 — who was he?
Dan Gurney: American racing driver, engineer and motorsport executive (1931–2018)
This colorless, highly flammable liquid with a sweet smell was once widely used as a general anesthetic before modern alternatives — what compound?
Defined in humans as an adult height of four foot ten or shorter, this condition's most common form — accounting for about 70% of cases — is a genetic disorder called achondroplasia. What is it?
Dwarfism: Small size of an organism, caused by growth deficiency or genetic mutations.
This Italian-American physicist discovered two elements, technetium and astatine, plus the antiproton — the last earning him a share of the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics. Who was he?
Emilio Segrè: Italian-American nuclear physicist and radiochemist (1905–1989)
Marketed under brand names like Arcoxia, this selective COX-2 inhibitor developed by Merck was approved in 63 countries by 2007 — everywhere, notably, except the United States — what is the drug?
This membranous bodily structure comes in superficial, visceral, and deep types, and a dangerous pressure buildup within it can cause compartment syndrome — what is it called?
Fascia: Layer of connective tissue in the body.

Members of this insect order have just one pair of true wings — the hindwings evolved into balance organs called halteres — and the group includes mosquitoes among its 150,000+ species. What are they commonly called?
Fly: Order of insects. A fly (pl. flies) is an insect of the order Diptera (from Ancient Greek δι- di- 'two' and πτερόν pteron 'wing'), named for the single pair of wings.
Caused by a loss of blood supply and marked by skin turning red or black, this condition comes in dry, wet, and gas forms — what is it?
Gangrene: Type of tissue death by ischemia.

Inducted into the U.S. Air Force Hall of Fame in 2018, this American mathematician modeled the precise shape of the Earth — work later baked into the Global Positioning System that now guides your phone. Who is she?
Known to the British as the Martlet, this American carrier-based fighter entered service in 1940 and remained the U.S. Navy's best fighter against the Mitsubishi Zero until mid-1943 — which aircraft?
Grumman F4F Wildcat: United States Navy World War II era fighter plane.
This German physicist was the first to conclusively demonstrate the electromagnetic waves predicted by James Clerk Maxwell's equations — who is he?
This genus of great apes emerged from Australopithecus and includes modern humans alongside extinct relatives, with chimpanzees and bonobos as its closest living kin — what genus is it?
Homo: Genus of hominins. Homo erectus and Homo neanderthalensis) classified as either ancestral or closely related to modern humans, collectively called archaic humans.

In this heart condition, the muscle walls, especially the wall between the ventricles, thicken without an obvious cause, weakening the heart's pumping and sometimes disrupting its electrical signals — which condition?

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Enlargement of the heart muscle. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM, or HOCM when obstructive) is a condition in which muscle tissues of the heart become thickened without an obvious cause.

This analytical framework describes how overlapping identities like race, gender, and class combine to create unique experiences of discrimination or privilege, and emerged partly as a critique of mainstream feminism — which concept?
Intersectionality: Theory of discrimination. The term intersectionality was coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989.
A Communist Party member and Stanford-trained psychiatrist, this woman is best remembered for her romantic relationship with J. Robert Oppenheimer, which put her under FBI surveillance. Who is she?
Personal physician to the Buddha and King Bimbisāra in 5th-century BCE Rājagṛha, this 'Medicine King' is still revered by traditional healers across Asia — who is he?

Jīvaka: Personal physician of the Buddha and Indian King Bimbisara. Jīvaka (Pali: Jīvaka Komārabhacca; Sanskrit: Jīvaka Kaumārabhṛtya) was the personal physician (Sanskrit: vaidya) of the Buddha and the Indian King Bimbisāra.
Named from Greek words for 'hare' and 'form,' this mammalian order splits into rabbits-and-hares on one branch and pikas on the other, totaling around 110 living species — which order?
Formed by cross-linking phenolic precursors, this class of complex organic polymers gives rigidity to plant cell walls, especially in wood and bark — what is it?
Lignin: Structural phenolic polymer in plant cell walls.
Native to Africa except for one species found only on Madagascar, this small parrot gets its common name from its strong, monogamous pair-bonding behavior — what is it?
Oblate rather than round, with a thin, loose peel that makes it easy to separate into segments, this citrus fruit is sweeter and stronger-tasting than its spherical, hybrid cousin — which fruit?
Mandarin orange: Small citrus fruit. A mandarin orange (Citrus reticulata), often simply called mandarin, is a small, rounded citrus tree fruit.
Its name means 'big tooth,' and this extinct giant mackerel shark — once mistaken for a great white relative — is known only from fragmentary remains. What is it?
Megalodon: Extinct giant shark species. Megalodon probably had a major impact on the structure of marine communities.
Sitting atop the brainstem and linking it to the diencephalon and cerebrum, this structure governs vision, hearing, motor control, and arousal -- what is it called?
Midbrain: Forward-most portion of the brainstem.

Nicknamed the Swiss cheese plant for its perforated leaves, this houseplant native to southern Mexico and Central America produces a fruit that's edible once ripe, despite needle-like calcium oxalate crystals elsewhere in the plant — what is its scientific name?
Monstera deliciosa: Species of plant. Monstera deliciosa, the Swiss cheese plant or split-leaf philodendron, is a species of flowering plant.
Made of the same tough protein as claws, hooves, and horns, this protective plate covers the tip of your fingers and toes — what is it?
Nail (anatomy): Hard keratin protection of digit.
Sold under the brand name Macrobid, this antibacterial drug treats lower urinary tract infections but isn't effective against kidney infections. What is it?
Nitrofurantoin: Antibacterial drug. Nitrofurantoin, sold under the brand name Macrobid among others, is an antibacterial medication of the nitrofuran class.

Sold under the brand name Zofran, this serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist prevents chemotherapy- and surgery-related nausea without the dopamine-blocking side effects that cause muscle restlessness — what is this drug?
Ondansetron: Medication to prevent nausea and vomiting.
Known for its fragrant leaves used to flavor dishes across Southeast Asia, Sri Lanka and Hainanese cuisine, this member of the screwpine genus is prized in many Asian kitchens — which plant?
Pandanus amaryllifolius: Species of tropical plant.
Developed at Abbott Laboratories in 1930 and nicknamed 'yellow jackets' for its brand-name capsule color, this barbiturate is used in veterinary euthanasia and some U.S. executions — what drug is it?
Cultivated since the days of the Inca Empire and known in English as the Cape gooseberry or goldenberry, this South American nightshade now grows wild worldwide — which species is it?
Physalis peruviana: Species of cultivated South American fruit. Physalis peruviana is a species of plant in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) native to Chile and Peru.

Derived from renewable resources such as corn starch and capable of biodegrading, this thermoplastic polyester made up about a quarter of the world's bioplastic market in 2022 — what compound is this?
Also called cherry laurel, this evergreen shrub native to the Black Sea region was once woven into wreaths for its resemblance to true bay laurel, though the two aren't closely related — which plant?
Prunus laurocerasus: Species of plant. It is not to be confused with its American relative Prunus caroliniana, which is also called cherry laurel.
The largest of the procyonid family, this North American mammal is famous for its facial mask, ringed tail, and remarkably dexterous front paws — which animal is it?
Raccoon: Medium-sized mammal native to North America.
Discovered in 1803 by William Hyde Wollaston and named for the rose color of one of its compounds, this rare silvery-white metal of the platinum group is used to enhance jewelry — which element?
Rhodium: Chemical element with atomic number 45 (Rh)
This Japanese botanist lived and worked during the Meiji era of the late 19th century — who was he?
Ryōkichi Yatabe: Japanese botanist and poet. Ryōkichi Yatabe (矢田部良吉; October 13, 1851 – August 8, 1899) was a Japanese botanist during the Meiji era.
Creator of a satirical comic strip about corporate cubicle life, this cartoonist also wrote the pandeistic novella 'God's Debris' — who is he?
Scott Adams: American cartoonist and author (1957–2026)
Named for a Swedish medical physicist, this SI unit measures the stochastic health risk of ionizing radiation, such as equivalent and effective dose — what unit is it?
Sievert: Derived SI unit of equivalent dose of ionizing radiation. One sievert equals 100 rem, which is an older, CGS radiation unit.
Native to the tropical Americas and a cousin of the cherimoya, which spiny fruit smells like pineapple and tastes like strawberries and apple with a sour citrus tang?
Soursop: Tropical fruit tree. Soursop (also called graviola, guyabano, and in Hispanic America guanábana) is the fruit of Annona muricata, a broadleaf, flowering, evergreen tree.
A member of the rose family, this bright red treat is botanically not a berry at all, and each of its 'seeds' on the outside is really a tiny fruit called an achene — what is it?
Strawberry: Edible fruit. The garden strawberry (or simply strawberry; Fragaria × ananassa) is a widely grown hybrid plant cultivated worldwide for its fruit.

This mammal family includes true digging specialists as well as aquatic desmans and the water-and-tunnel-adept star-nosed species, absent from Ireland but found from Eurasia to as far south as tropical Southeast Asian mountains — which family?
Talpidae: Family of small insectivorous mammals.

Comprising two Einstein-authored physics frameworks published in 1905 and 1915 — one covering phenomena without gravity, the other explaining gravitation itself — this pair introduced four-dimensional spacetime and superseded Newtonian mechanics. Which pair of physics frameworks is this?
Theory of relativity: Two interrelated physics theories by Albert Einstein.
This shelled reptile retracts its head and neck straight back into its shell for protection, with the largest species growing over a metre long and weighing more than 100 kilograms — what is it?
Named from the Greek word for cheese after being first isolated from casein in 1846, this amino acid carries the one-letter code Y — what is it?
Tyrosine: Amino acid. L-Tyrosine or tyrosine (symbol Tyr or Y) or 4-hydroxyphenylalanine is one of the 20 standard amino acids that are used by cells to synthesize proteins.

First glimpsed through Dmitri Ivanovsky's 1892 study of an ailing tobacco plant, this is the most numerous biological entity on Earth — yet it can only replicate inside another organism's living cells. What is it?
Virus: Infectious agent that replicates in cells.
This English economist and physician first made his name surveying Irish land to parcel out to Cromwell's soldiers, and is best remembered for his theories of 'political arithmetic' — who is it?
William Petty: English economist and philosopher (1623–1687)
The symbol for praseodymium is Pr. Praseodymium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pr and atomic number 59.
Rhenium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for rhenium is Re. Rhenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Re and atomic number 75.

In what year was Halle Berry born?
Halle Berry: Halle Maria Berry ( HAL-ee; born Maria Halle Berry; August 14, 1966) is an American actress.
In what year was Liza Minnelli born?
Liza Minnelli: Liza May Minnelli ( LY-zə; born March 12, 1946) is an American actress, singer, and dancer.
In what year was Robert Duvall born?
Robert Duvall: Duvall won the Academy Award for Best Actor for his performance as an alcoholic former country music star in Tender Mercies (1983).
In what year was Rob Schneider born?
Rob Schneider: Robert Michael Schneider ( SHNY-dər; born October 31, 1963) is an American actor and comedian.
In what year was Jenna Ortega born?
Jenna Ortega: Jenna Marie Ortega (born September 27, 2002) is an American actress.

Anne Heche: Heche's profile rose in 1997 with appearances in Donnie Brasco, Volcano, I Know What You Did Last Summer, and Wag the Dog.
